title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
summary: Specifies DHCPv6, which lets servers hand out configuration such as IPv6 addresses and other parameters to IPv6 hosts. It can allocate reusable addresses automatically and offers extra configuration flexibility. It is the stateful counterpart to stateless address autoconfiguration and can be used with it. It was replaced by RFC 8415.

plainLanguage.summary: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) lets a network assign IPv6 addresses and provide other settings to devices. Clients discover servers, request configuration, and contact a server later to extend address lifetimes.

questions: how do ipv6 hosts get addresses from a server
what is a duid in dhcpv6
subtitle: The original DHCPv6 protocol for managed IPv6 addresses and configuration.

tldr.problem: IPv6 devices need a way to obtain managed addresses and configuration such as DNS server information from a network.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPv6 clients discover servers over UDP, request addresses or settings, and renew address lifetimes. Relay agents can carry messages to servers on other links.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3315 has been obsoleted by RFC 8415 and updated by RFCs 4361, 5494, 6221, 6422, 6644, 7083, 7227, 7283 and 7550.

sections.title: What DHCPv6 Provides
sections.content:
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for Internet Protocol version 6 (DHCPv6) is a client/server protocol for managed configuration of IPv6 devices. A server can assign addresses and return other configuration in options; new options can extend the information carried by the protocol.

Clients use UDP and usually send messages to the link-scoped multicast address FF02::1:2, so they do not need a server address in advance. A relay agent on the client's link can pass messages to a server elsewhere, without changing what the client sees.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can ask a DHCPv6 server for an address and other network settings. It can send that request to a local multicast address without knowing the server's address.

sections.title: Finding a Server and Getting an Address
sections.content:
For settings without address assignment, the client sends Information-Request and receives Reply. To request addresses, the usual exchange is Solicit, Advertise, Request, and Reply: the client finds servers, chooses one, and asks it to confirm the assignment. If both sides use Rapid Commit, Solicit can be followed directly by Reply.

Each assigned address has preferred and valid lifetimes. The client sends Renew to the server that assigned it; if that server does not answer by the Rebind time, the client can ask any available server. Confirm checks whether addresses still fit a link, while Release and Decline report that addresses are no longer used or already in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can ask for settings alone or follow a four-message exchange to receive addresses. Later it renews the assignment with its server, or asks another server if the first does not answer.

sections.title: Messages, Options and Relays
sections.content:
Client and server messages start with a one-octet message type and a three-octet transaction ID, followed by options. The transaction ID lets the client match a reply to its request. Options carry values such as client identifiers and address assignments.

Clients listen on UDP port 546; servers and relay agents listen on port 547. A relay uses Relay-forward to wrap a client message and Relay-reply to return the server's answer. Relay headers include the link address and peer address, and the hop count is limited to 32.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message begins with a code for its type and a transaction number. Labeled options carry the configuration, while relay agents wrap messages when a server is on another link.

sections.title: Client Identifiers and Identity Associations
sections.content:
Each client and server has a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID). Peers treat it as an opaque value and compare it only for equality; the RFC says it should remain stable when network hardware changes. The defined DUID forms use a link-layer address and time, a vendor identifier, or a link-layer address.

An identity association (IA) groups related addresses assigned to one client interface. The client chooses an identity association identifier (IAID) for each IA and must keep that identifier consistent across restarts. An IA can hold non-temporary addresses or temporary addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A DUID gives a client or server a stable identifier. An identity association groups addresses for one interface, and its IAID identifies that group.

sections.title: Reliability and Authentication
sections.content:
Because DHCP uses UDP, clients retransmit requests when they do not receive expected replies. The retransmission time includes a random factor between -0.1 and +0.1 to reduce synchronized requests from many clients.

The RFC describes threats from malicious or mistaken servers, clients impersonating others, and denial-of-service attempts. DHCP authentication can authenticate participants and protect message integrity, but it does not provide privacy. A client must discard a Reconfigure message that is not authenticated or fails authentication validation.
sections.plainLanguage: A client repeats a request if no answer arrives, with random timing to avoid many devices retrying together. Authentication can verify who sent a message and whether it changed, but it does not hide the message contents.
